decks.title: Factorisation — Part 1: Common factors, grouping and the difference of two squares
goals: Say what factorising means and check it by multiplying back
Take out a common monomial or binomial factor, including after a change of sign
Factorise a difference of two squares, including after rearranging

slides.heading: Factorisation, Part 1
slides.body_md: Factorising writes an expression as a **product**. It undoes multiplying out.

visual.alt: Table with four rows pairing a product of factors with its expansion, such as three x times x plus four giving three x squared plus twelve x. Reading left to right is multiplying; reading right to left is factorising.
visual.caption: Multiplying out and factorising are opposite processes.

slides.narration: Welcome to factorisation. Multiplying out turns a product into a sum of terms. Factorising goes the other way: it writes a sum of terms as a product. In this part we use common factors, grouping, and the difference of two squares. After every factorisation, multiply back to check.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: **Take out** a common factor, even a bracket
Rearrange terms so that a method works
slides.narration: These are your goals for part one. You will take out common factors, including common brackets. You will group four terms in pairs, and spot a difference of two squares, even when the terms need rearranging first. And you will always check by multiplying back.

slides.heading: What is factorising?
slides.body_md: The **factors** of an expression are the expressions that multiply to give it. $3x(x + 4) = 3x^2 + 12x$, so $3x$ and $x + 4$ are factors of $3x^2 + 12x$.

visual.alt: A rectangle of width x plus four and height three x, cut by a vertical line into two parts of areas three x squared and twelve x.
visual.caption: The rectangle with sides $3x$ and $(x + 4)$ has area $3x^2 + 12x = 3x(x + 4)$.

slides.narration: Look at the rectangle. Its sides are three x and x plus four, so its area is the product. Cut it in two, and the pieces have areas three x squared and twelve x. So three x squared plus twelve x equals three x times x plus four. Writing it this way is called factorising.

slides.heading: Highest common factor of terms
slides.body_md: The **highest common factor** (HCF) of several terms is the largest number and the lowest power of each letter that divide every term. For $18p^2q^3$, $24pq^2$ and $30p^3q$ it is $6pq$.

visual.alt: Table finding the highest common factor of eighteen p squared q cubed, twenty-four p q squared and thirty p cubed q: the number six, the lowest power of p which is p, and the lowest power of q which is q, so six p q.
visual.caption: Take the largest common number and the lowest power of each letter.

slides.narration: To find the highest common factor of terms, take the largest number that divides all the coefficients, and the lowest power of each letter. For eighteen p squared q cubed, twenty four p q squared and thirty p cubed q, the number is six, the lowest power of p is p, and of q is q. So the factor is six p q.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: taking out the common factor
bullets: **Step 1 —** HCF of $36$, $54$, $18$ is $18$; of the letters, $xy$. So the HCF is $18xy$.
**Answer —** $18xy(2x^2 - 3xy + 1)$. The last term leaves $1$, not nothing.

visual.alt: Table dividing each term of thirty-six x cubed y minus fifty-four x squared y squared plus eighteen x y by the highest common factor eighteen x y, giving two x squared, minus three x y and one, so the factorised form is eighteen x y times the bracket.
visual.caption: Dividing each term by $18xy$ gives the bracket.

slides.narration: The highest common factor is eighteen x y. Divide each term by it. Thirty six x cubed y gives two x squared. Minus fifty four x squared y squared gives minus three x y. And eighteen x y gives one. Do not forget that one. The answer is eighteen x y times two x squared minus three x y plus one.

slides.heading: Quick check: highest common factor
slides.body_md: Take the lowest power of each letter.
slides.narration: Find the largest number that divides all three coefficients. Then take the lowest power of p and of q that appears in the three terms.

slides.heading: A common bracket and a change of sign
slides.body_md: A bracket can be a common factor: $7p(2x - y) + 3q(2x - y) = (2x - y)(7p + 3q)$. If a bracket appears reversed, use $b - a = -(a - b)$ to make it match.

visual.alt: Table of three expressions with a common binomial factor. In the second and third, a bracket appears with its terms in the opposite order, so a minus sign is taken out first before the common bracket is taken out.
visual.caption: Reverse the order of a bracket by taking out a minus sign.

slides.narration: A whole bracket can be the common factor. Seven p times two x minus y plus three q times the same bracket gives the bracket times seven p plus three q. If the bracket is written the other way round, take out a minus sign: y minus two x is minus two x minus y. Then the brackets match, and the sign moves to the front of the term.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a reversed bracket

visual.alt: Two steps for four m times three a minus five b plus nine n times five b minus three a: change five b minus three a into minus three a minus five b, then take out the common bracket three a minus five b to get three a minus five b times four m minus nine n.
visual.caption: A sign change makes the two brackets match.

slides.narration: The second bracket, five b minus three a, is the first bracket reversed. Write it as minus three a minus five b. That turns plus nine n into minus nine n. Now both terms contain the bracket three a minus five b, and the answer is that bracket times four m minus nine n.

slides.heading: Quick check: change of sign
slides.body_md: Which bracket is common once the sign is fixed?
slides.narration: Rewrite the bracket b minus a as minus a minus b. Then take out the common bracket, and watch the sign in front of the second term.

slides.heading: Factorising by grouping
slides.body_md: When four terms have no overall common factor, **group them in pairs**, take out each pair's common factor, and hope for a **common bracket**.

rows: Take out each pair's common factor
$(ax + ay) + (bx + by) = a(x + y) + b(x + y)$

visual.alt: Three steps for factorising a x plus a y plus b x plus b y by grouping: pair the terms, take a common factor from each pair, then take out the common bracket x plus y to get a plus b times x plus y.
visual.caption: Grouping in pairs when four terms have no overall common factor.

slides.narration: With four terms and no overall common factor, try grouping. Pair the terms so that each pair has a common factor. Take that factor out of each pair. If the same bracket appears twice, take it out, and you are done. In the example, a x plus a y gives a times x plus y, and b x plus b y gives b times x plus y.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a minus sign between the pairs
bullets: **Step 2 —** $-15yp - 10yq = -5y(3p + 2q)$. Take out $-5y$ so that the bracket matches.

visual.alt: Three steps for six x p plus four x q minus fifteen y p minus ten y q: the first pair has factor two x, the second pair has factor five y, both leave the bracket three p plus two q, giving two x minus five y times three p plus two q.
visual.caption: Grouping with a minus sign between the pairs.

slides.narration: The first pair has the common factor two x, and leaves three p plus two q. For the second pair, take out minus five y, not plus five y. That leaves the same bracket, three p plus two q. Now take the bracket out: the answer is two x minus five y times three p plus two q.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: rearranging first
bullets: **Step 1 —** The terms $pq$ and $-6$ share nothing, so rearrange: $pq + 2p - 3q - 6$.

visual.alt: Three steps for p q minus six plus two p minus three q: rearrange so that p q and two p come together, group as p times q plus two minus three times q plus two, and take out the bracket to get p minus three times q plus two.
visual.caption: Rearranging the terms so that grouping works.

slides.narration: The terms as they stand do not pair up well. Rearrange them so that p q and two p come together, and minus three q and minus six come together. The first pair gives p times q plus two. The second gives minus three times q plus two. The answer is p minus three times q plus two.

slides.heading: The difference of two squares
slides.body_md: $a^2 - b^2 = (a - b)(a + b)$. Cut a small square $b \times b$ from a square $a \times a$ and rearrange the pieces into a rectangle $(a - b)$ by $(a + b)$.

visual.alt: A square of side a with a small square of side b cut from one corner, shaded, beside a rectangle of length a plus b and height a minus b. The two shapes have the same area, so a squared minus b squared equals a minus b times a plus b.
visual.caption: The shaded piece, $a^2 - b^2$, can be cut and rearranged into a rectangle $(a - b)$ by $(a + b)$.

slides.narration: Take a square of side a and cut a small square of side b from a corner. What is left has area a squared minus b squared. Cut and move one strip, and it forms a rectangle of length a plus b and height a minus b. So a squared minus b squared equals a minus b times a plus b. There is no middle term.

slides.heading: Spotting perfect squares
slides.body_md: A term is a **perfect square** when its number is a square and every power of a letter is even. $x^2 - y^2$ needs **two** squares and a **minus** sign. A **sum** of two squares, like $x^2 + 9$, does not factorise.

visual.alt: Table testing six terms for being perfect squares: twenty-five m squared has root five m, thirty-six n to the fourth has root six n squared, eight x squared is not, forty-nine has root seven, twelve is not, and p to the sixth has root p cubed.
visual.caption: A term is a perfect square when its number is a square and every power is even.

slides.narration: Before using the difference of squares, check that both terms are perfect squares. Twenty five m squared is five m all squared. Thirty six n to the fourth is six n squared, all squared. Eight x squared is not a square, because eight is not. And the sign must be a minus. A sum of two squares does not factorise in this way.

slides.heading: Quick check: which is a difference of two squares?
slides.body_md: Test both terms and the sign.
slides.narration: Check each option. Both terms must be perfect squares, the number and every power, and the sign between them must be a minus.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: common factor, then squares

visual.alt: Four steps for seventy-two x cubed minus ninety-eight x y squared: take out two x, recognise thirty-six x squared minus forty-nine y squared as a difference of squares, and write the answer two x times six x minus seven y times six x plus seven y.
visual.caption: Common factor first, then the difference of squares.

slides.narration: Always look for a common factor first. Seventy two x cubed minus ninety eight x y squared has the common factor two x. What is left, thirty six x squared minus forty nine y squared, is a difference of two squares: six x all squared minus seven y all squared. So the complete answer is two x times six x minus seven y times six x plus seven y.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: rearranging into a difference of squares
bullets: **Step 1 —** Take a minus sign out of the last three terms: $x^2 - (y^2 + 2y + 1)$. Every sign inside changes.

visual.alt: Three steps for x squared minus y squared minus two y minus one: take a minus sign out of the last three terms, recognise y squared plus two y plus one as y plus one squared, and use a difference of squares to get x minus y minus one times x plus y plus one.
visual.caption: Rearranging into a difference of squares.

slides.narration: Here three terms with y make a perfect square, but only after taking out a minus sign. Minus y squared minus two y minus one is minus the bracket y squared plus two y plus one. That bracket is y plus one all squared. Now we have x squared minus y plus one squared, a difference of squares, giving x minus y minus one times x plus y plus one.

slides.heading: Quick check: grouping, then squares
slides.narration: Look at the first three terms. Do they form a perfect square? If so, the whole expression may be a difference of two squares.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: using the identity twice
bullets: **Answer —** $(2p - 3q)(2p + 3q)(4p^2 + 9q^2)$. The last bracket is a sum of squares and stays.

visual.alt: Four steps for sixteen p to the fourth minus eighty-one q to the fourth: write it as four p squared squared minus nine q squared squared, factorise, then factorise four p squared minus nine q squared again, while four p squared plus nine q squared cannot be split.
visual.caption: A difference of squares may need to be used twice.

slides.narration: Sixteen p to the fourth is four p squared, squared. Eighty one q to the fourth is nine q squared, squared. So the first step gives four p squared minus nine q squared times four p squared plus nine q squared. The first bracket is again a difference of squares. The second, a sum of squares, cannot be split. So there are three factors in the answer.

slides.heading: Shortcuts for numbers
slides.body_md: The identity makes some number work easy: $63^2 - 37^2 = (63 - 37)(63 + 37) = 26 \times 100 = 2600$.

visual.alt: Table of three number calculations done with a difference of squares: sixty-three squared minus thirty-seven squared is twenty-six times one hundred, which is two thousand six hundred; one hundred twenty-five squared minus twenty-five squared is one hundred times one hundred fifty; eighty-seven squared minus thirteen squared is seventy-four times one hundred.
visual.caption: Factorising makes number calculations short.

slides.narration: The identity is also a calculation shortcut. Sixty three squared minus thirty seven squared is sixty three minus thirty seven, which is twenty six, times sixty three plus thirty seven, which is one hundred. So the answer is two thousand six hundred, with no big squares needed. The same works for any two numbers.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Always take out the **common factor** first
$a^2 - b^2 = (a - b)(a + b)$; a **sum** of squares does not factorise

visual.alt: Summary table for part one: take out a common factor, change the order of a bracket with a minus sign, group four terms in pairs, and factorise a difference of two squares.
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance.

slides.narration: To sum up part one. Take out the common factor first. A reversed bracket becomes a match when you take out a minus sign. Four terms are grouped in pairs. A difference of two squares factorises as a minus b times a plus b, but a sum of squares does not. And always multiply back to check.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Common factor (2 marks):** highest common factor 1 + bracket 1
**Grouping (3 marks):** pairs 1 + common bracket 1 + final product 1
**Difference of squares (2–3 marks):** common factor 1 + squares recognised 1 + result 1
**Mistake:** dropping the $1$ when a term equals the common factor
**Mistake:** forgetting to change every sign inside a bracket after taking out a minus
**Mistake:** stopping while a bracket still has a common factor
slides.narration: In the examination, show each step: the common factor, the grouped pairs, the squares you recognise. Do not drop a term that leaves one. When you take out a minus sign, change every sign inside the bracket. And finish the job: look at each bracket and ask whether it can be factorised further.

decks.title: Factorisation — Part 2: Cubes, quadratic trinomials and mixed methods
goals: Factorise the sum and difference of two cubes
Factorise ax squared plus bx plus c by splitting the middle term, including two letters and perfect squares
Combine methods in the right order
Find and correct errors in a factorisation

slides.heading: Factorisation, Part 2

visual.alt: Table of the cubes of the numbers one to ten: one, eight, twenty-seven, sixty-four, one hundred twenty-five, two hundred sixteen, three hundred forty-three, five hundred twelve, seven hundred twenty-nine and one thousand.
visual.caption: Cubes worth knowing.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two of factorisation. Here we meet the sum and difference of two cubes, and quadratic trinomials, which are factorised by splitting the middle term. At the end we combine all the methods and learn to find errors. The table shows the cubes of the numbers one to ten, which are worth knowing.

slides.heading: The sum and difference of two cubes
slides.body_md: $a^3 + b^3 = (a + b)(a^2 - ab + b^2)$ and $a^3 - b^3 = (a - b)(a^2 + ab + b^2)$. The first bracket copies the sign; in the second, the middle sign is opposite and the last term is always **plus**.

visual.alt: Table of the two cube identities: a cubed plus b cubed equals a plus b times a squared minus a b plus b squared, and a cubed minus b cubed equals a minus b times a squared plus a b plus b squared.
visual.caption: The signs: the first bracket copies the sign; in the second bracket the middle sign is the opposite and the last term is always plus.

slides.narration: Here are the two cube identities. For a sum of cubes, the first bracket is a plus b, and the second is a squared minus a b plus b squared. For a difference, the first bracket is a minus b, and the second is a squared plus a b plus b squared. A memory aid: same sign, opposite sign, always plus.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a sum of cubes

visual.alt: Three steps for twenty-seven m cubed plus sixty-four n cubed: write it as three m cubed plus four n cubed, build the second factor nine m squared minus twelve m n plus sixteen n squared, and write the product.
visual.caption: Sum of two cubes with $a = 3m$ and $b = 4n$.

slides.narration: First recognise the cubes. Twenty seven m cubed is three m all cubed, and sixty four n cubed is four n all cubed. So a is three m and b is four n. The second bracket is a squared, which is nine m squared, minus a b, which is twelve m n, plus b squared, which is sixteen n squared. Multiply back to check.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a difference of cubes

visual.alt: Three steps for one thousand minus twenty-seven y cubed: write it as ten cubed minus three y cubed, build the second factor one hundred plus thirty y plus nine y squared, and write the product ten minus three y times that.
visual.caption: Difference of two cubes with $a = 10$ and $b = 3y$.

slides.narration: One thousand is ten cubed, and twenty seven y cubed is three y all cubed. So a is ten and b is three y. For a difference, the first bracket is a minus b, which is ten minus three y. The second bracket is one hundred plus thirty y plus nine y squared. The middle term is plus this time.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: common factor first

visual.alt: Three steps for five x to the fourth plus forty x: take out five x, factorise x cubed plus eight as x plus two times x squared minus two x plus four, and write the complete answer.
visual.caption: Common factor first, then a sum of cubes.

slides.narration: There is no cube in sight at first, because five x to the fourth is not a cube. But take out the common factor five x. What remains is x cubed plus eight, a sum of cubes. It factorises as x plus two times x squared minus two x plus four. The complete answer has three factors.

slides.heading: Quick check: common factor and cubes
slides.narration: Look for a common factor before anything else. Then see whether what is left is a sum or a difference of two cubes.

slides.heading: Cubes and the values of $x + y$ and $xy$
slides.body_md: Because $x^3 + y^3 = (x + y)(x^2 - xy + y^2)$ and $x^2 + y^2 = (x + y)^2 - 2xy$, we can find $x^3 + y^3$ from $x + y$ and $xy$ alone.

visual.alt: Table of four steps finding x cubed plus y cubed when x plus y is five and x y is four: factorise, find x squared plus y squared as twenty-five minus eight which is seventeen, the second factor is thirteen, and the value is sixty-five.
visual.caption: Using $x + y = 5$ and $xy = 4$.

slides.narration: Suppose x plus y is five and x y is four. We do not need x and y themselves. Use the factorised form. First, x squared plus y squared is five squared minus two times four, which is seventeen. The second factor is seventeen minus four, thirteen. So the sum of cubes is five times thirteen, sixty five.

slides.heading: Splitting the middle term: a trinomial with $a = 1$
slides.body_md: To factorise $x^2 + bx + c$, find two numbers with **sum $b$** and **product $c$**, and split $bx$ into those two terms.

visual.alt: Table of the factor pairs of forty with their sums: one and forty give forty-one, two and twenty give twenty-two, four and ten give fourteen, and five and eight give thirteen, which is the number needed.
visual.caption: For $x^2 + 13x + 40$ we need two numbers with product $40$ and sum $13$.

slides.narration: To factorise x squared plus b x plus c, find two numbers whose sum is b and whose product is c. For x squared plus thirteen x plus forty, list the factor pairs of forty and their sums. One and forty give forty one. Two and twenty give twenty two. Four and ten give fourteen. Five and eight give thirteen. That is our pair.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: splitting the middle term
bullets: **Answer —** $(x + 5)(x + 8)$. The area model shows the four parts $x^2$, $8x$, $5x$, $40$.

visual.alt: A rectangle with width x plus eight and height x plus five divided into four parts with areas x squared, eight x, five x and forty.
visual.caption: $x^2 + 8x + 5x + 40 = (x + 5)(x + 8)$.

slides.narration: Split thirteen x into five x and eight x. Then group: x times x plus five, plus eight times x plus five. The bracket x plus five is common, so the answer is x plus five times x plus eight. The picture shows why: a rectangle with sides x plus five and x plus eight has four parts, with areas x squared, eight x, five x and forty.

slides.heading: Signs of the two numbers
slides.body_md: If $c > 0$ the two numbers have the **same sign** as $b$. If $c < 0$ they have **opposite signs**, and the larger number (in size) takes the sign of $b$.

visual.alt: Table with four trinomials showing how the signs of the two numbers depend on the signs of the middle and last terms: both positive, both negative, or one of each with the larger one taking the sign of the middle term.
visual.caption: Signs of the two numbers: product positive means the same sign; product negative means opposite signs.

slides.narration: The signs of the two numbers depend on b and c. If c is positive, the numbers have the same sign, both positive if b is positive and both negative if b is negative. If c is negative, they have opposite signs, and the larger one in size takes the sign of b. The table shows four trinomials on the same pair of numbers.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: negative numbers
bullets: **First —** product $60$ is positive, sum $-17$ negative: both negative, $-5$ and $-12$. $(x - 5)(x - 12)$.
**Second —** product $-45$ is negative: opposite signs, $9$ and $-5$ (sum $4$). $(x + 9)(x - 5)$.

rows: Group and take out the bracket
Group and take out the bracket

visual.alt: Two trinomials. For x squared minus seventeen x plus sixty, both numbers are negative: minus five and minus twelve. For x squared plus four x minus forty-five, the numbers have opposite signs: nine and minus five.
visual.caption: Splitting with negative numbers.

slides.narration: First, x squared minus seventeen x plus sixty. The product is positive and the sum is negative, so both numbers are negative: minus five and minus twelve. Second, x squared plus four x minus forty five. The product is negative, so the signs differ, and the larger number, nine, takes the plus sign of the middle term. The pair is nine and minus five.

slides.heading: When the coefficient of $x^2$ is not $1$
slides.body_md: For $ax^2 + bx + c$, find two numbers with **sum $b$** and **product $ac$**. For $6x^2 + 17x + 12$: $ac = 72$, and $8 + 9 = 17$.

visual.alt: A rectangle with width three x plus four and height two x plus three, divided into four parts with areas six x squared, eight x, nine x and twelve.
visual.caption: $6x^2 + 8x + 9x + 12 = (2x + 3)(3x + 4)$.

slides.narration: When the coefficient of x squared is not one, the product of the two numbers must be a times c. For six x squared plus seventeen x plus twelve, a c is seventy two. Two numbers with sum seventeen and product seventy two are eight and nine. Split, group, and take out the bracket. The picture shows the four parts of the rectangle.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: a trinomial with $a > 1$

visual.alt: Five steps for eight x squared minus twenty-two x plus fifteen: the product is one hundred twenty, the pair is minus ten and minus twelve, split, group as two x times four x minus five minus three times four x minus five, and take out the bracket.
visual.caption: Both numbers negative because $ac > 0$ and $b < 0$.

slides.narration: The product a c is one hundred twenty and the sum is minus twenty two, so both numbers are negative: minus ten and minus twelve. Split the middle term, then group. Two x times four x minus five, minus three times four x minus five. The common bracket is four x minus five, and the answer is two x minus three times four x minus five.

slides.heading: Quick check: splitting the middle term
slides.narration: The two numbers must add to the coefficient of x and multiply to the constant term. Test each option on both conditions.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: two letters

visual.alt: Four steps for six x squared minus x y minus twelve y squared: the product of six and minus twelve is minus seventy-two, the pair is eight and minus nine, split, group, and take out the bracket to get two x minus three y times three x plus four y.
visual.caption: A trinomial in $x$ and $y$.

slides.narration: With two letters, the method does not change. The product of six and minus twelve is minus seventy two, and the middle coefficient is minus one. The numbers eight and minus nine have product minus seventy two and sum minus one. Split, group, and take out the bracket three x plus four y. The answer is two x minus three y times three x plus four y.

slides.heading: Perfect-square trinomials
slides.body_md: $a^2 + 2ab + b^2 = (a + b)^2$ and $a^2 - 2ab + b^2 = (a - b)^2$. Test: first and last terms are perfect squares and the middle term is twice the product of their roots.

visual.alt: A square with side five x plus four divided into four parts with areas twenty-five x squared, twenty x, twenty x and sixteen.
visual.caption: $25x^2 + 20x + 20x + 16 = (5x + 4)^2$.

slides.narration: Some trinomials are perfect squares. Twenty five x squared plus forty x plus sixteen has first term five x squared and last term four squared, and the middle term is two times five x times four, which is forty x. So it is five x plus four, all squared. The picture shows a square of side five x plus four.

slides.heading: Choosing the order of methods
slides.body_md: Always begin with the **common factor**, then count the terms. Finish by looking at every bracket again.

nodes.label: Two terms: difference of squares, or sum or difference of cubes
Three terms: split the middle term or spot a perfect square
Look again: can any bracket be split further?

visual.alt: Flow chart for choosing a factorising method: take out any common factor, count the terms, use squares or cubes for two terms, split the middle term for three terms, group for four terms, look again for further factors, and multiply back to check.
visual.caption: Choosing a method.

slides.narration: Here is a plan. First take out any common factor. Then count the terms. Two terms: look for a difference of squares or a sum or difference of cubes. Three terms: split the middle term or spot a perfect square. Four terms: group in pairs. Then look at every bracket again to see if it can be split further, and finally multiply back to check.

slides.heading: Worked example 8: two methods in sequence

visual.alt: Two mixed examples. First take out three x, then split the trinomial with the pair minus six and two. Second, group the first three terms as x plus five squared, and use a difference of squares with four y.
visual.caption: Two methods in sequence.

slides.narration: Two examples with two methods each. In the first, take out three x, then split the trinomial with the pair minus six and two. In the second, the first three terms are x plus five all squared, so the whole expression is a difference of two squares with four y. The answer has the brackets x plus five minus four y, and x plus five plus four y.

slides.heading: Finding errors in a factorisation
slides.body_md: Check a claim by **multiplying back**. If the product differs, the factorisation is **wrong**. If it matches but a bracket has a common factor, it is **incomplete**.

visual.alt: Table checking four claimed factorisations by multiplying back. The first two give a different expression and are wrong; the third multiplies back correctly but still has a common factor two in the first bracket; the fourth is correct and complete.
visual.caption: Check a factorisation by multiplying back, then look for a common factor.

slides.narration: To check a factorisation, multiply back. If you get a different expression, the claim is wrong. In the table, the first two claims fail. If the product is right but a bracket still has a common factor, the factorisation is incomplete. Two x minus six has the common factor two. The last claim is both correct and complete.

slides.heading: Quick check: spot the error
slides.narration: Expand the product to see whether it matches. Then look at each bracket for a common factor. Choose the statement that is true on both counts.

sections.heading: 1. Factors, factorising and multiplying back
sections.body_md:
To **factorise** an expression is to write it as a **product** of simpler expressions (its factors). It reverses multiplying out, so every factorisation can be **checked by multiplying back**.

- $3x(x + 4) = 3x^2 + 12x$, so $3x^2 + 12x$ factorises as $3x(x + 4)$.
- A factorisation is **complete** when no bracket has a common factor and no bracket can be split further.
- Always begin by taking out the **common factor**; the other methods work on what is left.

key_terms.definition_md: Write an expression as a product of factors.
A product in which no bracket has a common factor or can be factorised further.

sections.heading: 2. Common factors and grouping
sections.body_md:
**Highest common factor (HCF) of terms:** the largest number dividing every coefficient and the lowest power of each letter: for $18p^2q^3$, $24pq^2$, $30p^3q$ it is $6pq$.

**Taking it out:** divide every term by the HCF; a term equal to the HCF leaves $1$: $36x^3y - 54x^2y^2 + 18xy = 18xy(2x^2 - 3xy + 1)$.

**Common bracket:** $7p(2x - y) + 3q(2x - y) = (2x - y)(7p + 3q)$. A reversed bracket is fixed with $b - a = -(a - b)$.

**Grouping (four terms):** pair the terms, take out each pair's factor, then the common bracket: $6xp + 4xq - 15yp - 10yq = 2x(3p + 2q) - 5y(3p + 2q) = (2x - 5y)(3p + 2q)$. Rearrange the terms first if the pairs do not match.

key_terms.definition_md: The largest number and the lowest power of each letter that divide every term.
Pairing the terms of a four-term expression so that a common bracket appears.

sections.heading: 3. Difference of two squares
sections.body_md:
$a^2 - b^2 = (a - b)(a + b)$. Both terms must be **perfect squares** (square coefficient, even powers) with a **minus** sign; a **sum** of two squares, such as $x^2 + 9$, does not factorise.

- With a common factor first: $72x^3 - 98xy^2 = 2x(6x - 7y)(6x + 7y)$.
- Rearranging: $x^2 - y^2 - 2y - 1 = x^2 - (y + 1)^2 = (x - y - 1)(x + y + 1)$. Taking out a minus sign changes **every** sign inside.
- Twice in a row: $16p^4 - 81q^4 = (2p - 3q)(2p + 3q)(4p^2 + 9q^2)$.
- Number shortcuts: $63^2 - 37^2 = 26 \times 100 = 2600$.

key_terms.definition_md: A term whose number is a square and whose letters have even powers, such as $25m^2$ or $36n^4$.
An expression $a^2 - b^2$, which equals $(a - b)(a + b)$.

sections.heading: 4. Sum and difference of two cubes
sections.body_md:
$a^3 + b^3 = (a + b)(a^2 - ab + b^2)$ and $a^3 - b^3 = (a - b)(a^2 + ab + b^2)$.

**Signs:** the first bracket copies the sign; in the quadratic bracket the middle sign is the opposite, and the last term is always plus. The quadratic factor does not split further.

- $27m^3 + 64n^3 = (3m + 4n)(9m^2 - 12mn + 16n^2)$.
- Take out a common factor first: $5x^4 + 40x = 5x(x + 2)(x^2 - 2x + 4)$.
- With $x + y = 5$ and $xy = 4$: $x^3 + y^3 = 5 \times (17 - 4) = 65$.

sections.heading: 5. Splitting the middle term when $a = 1$
sections.body_md:
To factorise $x^2 + bx + c$ find two numbers $p$ and $q$ with **$p + q = b$** and **$pq = c$**, then write $bx = px + qx$ and group.

- $x^2 + 13x + 40$: the pair is $5$ and $8$; $x^2 + 5x + 8x + 40 = x(x + 5) + 8(x + 5) = (x + 5)(x + 8)$.
- **Signs:** if $c > 0$ both numbers have the sign of $b$; if $c < 0$ the numbers have opposite signs and the larger (in size) takes the sign of $b$.
- $x^2 - 17x + 60 = (x - 5)(x - 12)$ and $x^2 + 4x - 45 = (x + 9)(x - 5)$.

key_terms.definition_md: Writing $bx$ as $px + qx$ with $p + q = b$ and $pq = ac$, then grouping.
An expression with three terms, such as $x^2 + 13x + 40$.

sections.heading: 6. Splitting the middle term when $a \ne 1$; two letters; perfect squares
sections.body_md:
For $ax^2 + bx + c$ the two numbers have **sum $b$** and **product $ac$**: $6x^2 + 17x + 12$ has $ac = 72$ and the pair $8$, $9$, so $6x^2 + 8x + 9x + 12 = 2x(3x + 4) + 3(3x + 4) = (2x + 3)(3x + 4)$.

- Two letters: $6x^2 - xy - 12y^2 = 6x^2 + 8xy - 9xy - 12y^2 = (2x - 3y)(3x + 4y)$.
- **Perfect squares:** $a^2 \pm 2ab + b^2 = (a \pm b)^2$: $25x^2 + 40x + 16 = (5x + 4)^2$.
- **A bracket as one letter:** $(a + b)^2 - 7(a + b) + 12 = (a + b - 3)(a + b - 4)$.
- A trinomial that does not split over the integers (no pair has the right sum and product), such as $x^2 + 6x + 10$, is left as it is.

sections.heading: 7. Mixed methods and checking
sections.body_md:
**Order:** (1) take out the common factor; (2) count the terms: two terms use squares or cubes, three terms split the middle term or spot a perfect square, four terms group; (3) look at every bracket again; (4) multiply back.

- $3x^3 - 12x^2 - 36x = 3x(x - 6)(x + 2)$ (common factor, then a trinomial).
- $x^2 + 10x + 25 - 16y^2 = (x + 5 - 4y)(x + 5 + 4y)$ (perfect square, then squares).
- $x^6 - 64 = (x - 2)(x^2 + 2x + 4)(x + 2)(x^2 - 2x + 4)$ (squares, then cubes).

**Finding errors:** multiply back. A different product means the factorisation is **wrong**; the same product with a common factor still in a bracket means it is **incomplete**: $(2x - 6)(x + 3)$ for $2x^2 - 18$ should be $2(x - 3)(x + 3)$.

key_terms.definition_md: A product that multiplies back correctly but has a bracket with a common factor or a bracket that can be split.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *Common factor (2 marks):* highest common factor 1; bracket 1.
- *Grouping (3 marks):* pairs 1; common bracket 1; final product 1.
- *Difference of squares (2–3 marks):* common factor 1; squares recognised 1; result 1.
- *Cubes (2–3 marks):* cubes identified 1; first bracket 1; second bracket 1.
- *Trinomial (3 marks):* pair with the right sum and product 1; grouped 1; factors 1.
- *10-mark structured question:* parts (a), (b), (c) usually 3 + 3 + 4; show every step.

**Common mistakes**
1. Dropping the $1$ when a term is equal to the common factor.
2. Changing only the first sign inside a bracket after taking out a minus sign.
3. Treating a sum of two squares, such as $x^2 + 16$, as if it factorised.
4. Using the wrong middle sign in the quadratic factor of a sum or difference of cubes.
5. Using $p + q = c$ instead of $pq = ac$ when splitting the middle term.
6. Stopping while a bracket still has a common factor, such as $(2x + 6)(x + 4)$.
7. Not multiplying back to check.

questions.stem_md: The highest common factor of the terms $18p^2q^3$, $24pq^2$ and $30p^3q$ is
questions.solution_md: The numerical HCF of $18$, $24$ and $30$ is $6$. The lowest power of $p$ is $p$ (in $24pq^2$) and the lowest power of $q$ is $q$ (in $30p^3q$). So the HCF is $6pq$. The option $360p^3q^3$ is the lowest common multiple, which takes the highest powers.

questions.stem_md: Dev takes out the greatest common factor from $15a^3b^2 - 35a^2b^3$. His result is
questions.solution_md: The HCF of the two terms is $5a^2b^2$, and $15a^3b^2 = 5a^2b^2 \times 3a$, $35a^2b^3 = 5a^2b^2 \times 7b$. So the expression is $5a^2b^2(3a - 7b)$. The second and fourth options multiply back to the same expression but leave a common factor inside the bracket, and the third has the wrong sign.

questions.stem_md: Four rectangular beds in a school garden have areas $4ax$, $6ay$, $2bx$ and $3by$ square metres. The total area, written as a product of two factors, is
questions.solution_md: Group the beds in pairs: $4ax + 6ay = 2a(2x + 3y)$ and $2bx + 3by = b(2x + 3y)$. The bracket $(2x + 3y)$ is common, so the total area is $(2a + b)(2x + 3y)$ square metres. The other options expand to $4ax + 4ay + 3bx + 3by$ and similar expressions that differ from the given total.

questions.stem_md: Written as a product, $5p(a - b) + 3q(b - a)$ is equal to
questions.solution_md: Since $b - a = -(a - b)$, the second term is $-3q(a - b)$. Now $(a - b)$ is a common factor: $5p(a - b) - 3q(a - b) = (a - b)(5p - 3q)$. Forgetting the change of sign gives the wrong option $(a - b)(5p + 3q)$.

questions.stem_md: Which of these expressions is a difference of two squares?
questions.solution_md: $36p^4 - 49q^2 = (6p^2)^2 - (7q)^2$ has two perfect squares with a minus sign between them. The second has a plus sign, $36p^3$ is not a perfect square because $3$ is odd, and $48$ is not a perfect square.

questions.stem_md: Using $a^2 - b^2 = (a - b)(a + b)$, Farida finds the value of $83^2 - 17^2$ without squaring either number. Her answer is
questions.solution_md: $83^2 - 17^2 = (83 - 17)(83 + 17) = 66 \times 100 = 6600$. The number $4356$ is $66^2$, which comes from forgetting to multiply by $83 + 17$.

questions.stem_md: Gurpreet must factorise $98x^2 - 8y^2$ completely. Which answer is correct?
questions.solution_md: Take out the common factor $2$ first: $98x^2 - 8y^2 = 2(49x^2 - 4y^2)$. Then $49x^2 - 4y^2 = (7x)^2 - (2y)^2 = (7x - 2y)(7x + 2y)$. So the complete factorisation is $2(7x - 2y)(7x + 2y)$. The second option has the same product but $14x - 4y$ still has the factor $2$; the third stops one step early.

questions.stem_md: Rewriting $x^2 - y^2 + 6y - 9$ as $x^2 - (y - 3)^2$ is the first step. The complete factorisation is
questions.solution_md: $x^2 - (y - 3)^2$ is a difference of two squares with $a = x$ and $b = y - 3$, so it equals $(x - (y - 3))(x + (y - 3)) = (x - y + 3)(x + y - 3)$. Take care with the sign: removing the bracket in $x - (y - 3)$ gives $x - y + 3$.

questions.stem_md: The factorisation of $8p^3 + 125q^3$ is
questions.solution_md: $8p^3 + 125q^3 = (2p)^3 + (5q)^3$. With $a = 2p$ and $b = 5q$, $a^3 + b^3 = (a + b)(a^2 - ab + b^2) = (2p + 5q)(4p^2 - 10pq + 25q^2)$. For a sum of cubes the middle term of the quadratic factor is negative.

questions.stem_md: Rohit's worksheet reads $64m^3 - 27 = (4m - 3)(\ldots)$. The missing factor is
questions.solution_md: $64m^3 - 27 = (4m)^3 - 3^3 = (4m - 3)(16m^2 + 12m + 9)$, because $(a - b)(a^2 + ab + b^2) = a^3 - b^3$ with $a = 4m$, $b = 3$ and $ab = 12m$. For a difference of cubes the middle term is positive.

questions.stem_md: Completely factorised, $2x^4 - 54x$ is
questions.solution_md: First take out the common factor $2x$: $2x^4 - 54x = 2x(x^3 - 27)$. Then $x^3 - 27 = x^3 - 3^3 = (x - 3)(x^2 + 3x + 9)$. So the complete factorisation is $2x(x - 3)(x^2 + 3x + 9)$. The second option stops after one step, and the third has the common factor $x$ still inside a bracket.

questions.stem_md: Rohit wants to factorise $x^2 + 11x + 28$ by splitting the middle term. He should write $11x$ as
questions.solution_md: We need two numbers whose sum is $11$ and whose product is $1 \times 28 = 28$. The pair $4$ and $7$ works: $4 + 7 = 11$ and $4 \times 7 = 28$. So $x^2 + 11x + 28 = x^2 + 4x + 7x + 28 = x(x + 4) + 7(x + 4) = (x + 4)(x + 7)$. The pair $2, 9$ has the right sum but the product $18$.

questions.stem_md: A student splits the middle term of $6y^2 - 7y - 20$ and gets two linear factors. They are
questions.solution_md: Here $ac = 6 \times (-20) = -120$ and $b = -7$. The pair $8$ and $-15$ has sum $-7$ and product $-120$. So $6y^2 - 7y - 20 = 6y^2 + 8y - 15y - 20 = 2y(3y + 4) - 5(3y + 4) = (2y - 5)(3y + 4)$. The option $(2y + 5)(3y - 4)$ gives $+7y$ instead.

questions.stem_md:
Three students made errors. Find each error and give the correct factorisation.

(a) Aarav wrote $x^3 + 27 = (x + 3)(x^2 + 3x + 9)$. [3]

(b) Bhavna wrote $4x^2 - 16y^2 = (2x - 4y)(2x + 4y)$ and stopped there. [3]

(c) Chirag wrote $x^2 - y^2 - 2y - 1 = x^2 - (y^2 - 2y - 1)$ and tried to carry on. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:

(b) The product is correct, but $2x - 4y = 2(x - 2y)$ and $2x + 4y = 2(x + 2y)$ still have a common factor. Correct: $4x^2 - 16y^2 = 4(x - 2y)(x + 2y)$.

(c) Taking a minus sign out of $-y^2 - 2y - 1$ changes every sign inside: $-y^2 - 2y - 1 = -(y^2 + 2y + 1)$, not $-(y^2 - 2y - 1)$. Correct: $x^2 - (y^2 + 2y + 1) = x^2 - (y + 1)^2 = (x - y - 1)(x + y + 1)$.
